metaTitle: Best Bench Vises for the Workshop
metaDescription: Seven bench vises compared on jaw width, opening, throat depth, ductile iron build, swivel locks and spindle design, with picks for a garage and a metal shop.
expertTake: The Wilton 746A 6 inch mechanics vise is our top pick for its enclosed greased spindle, replaceable hardened jaws and a solid swivel base. The VEVOR 6 inch vise is the value pick, a ductile iron body with an anvil at a low cost. Anyone who mounts to a thin or hollow bench top should skip heavy vises until the bench is reinforced.
introParagraphs: A bench vise is the second pair of hands in a workshop. It clamps stock firmly so you can saw, file, drill or bend without the work moving, and it stands up to far more force than a clamp.

Jaw width, opening and body material set what a vise can hold and how long it lasts. Listings tout clamping force in tens of thousands of pounds, which we treat with caution. This guide compares seven vises and explains how to match one to your bench.

products.name: Wilton 746A 6 inch mechanics bench vise, enclosed spindle, pipe jaws
products.description:
The Wilton 746A is a 6 inch mechanics vise with a fully enclosed spindle, sealed in grease so that chips and dust stay out of the screw and nut. Replaceable hardened steel jaw faces grip flat stock, and built in pipe jaws hold round work.

The jaw opening is 5 3/4 inches and the throat depth is 4 1/8 inches, giving the capacity most garage jobs need. The 360 degree swivel base has double lockdowns, which keep the vise from rotating under load. Compared with import ductile iron vises, the 746A has a more serious spindle and tighter tolerances. Compared with the Forward CR80A, it is smaller and cheaper but not as massive.

Ownership is simple. Mount it through the bench with bolts and a backing plate, keep the sliding surfaces lightly oiled and replace jaw faces when the serrations flatten. A sealed spindle needs little attention, which is a real advantage in a dusty shop.
products.bestFor: Home mechanics and metal workers who want a durable all round 6 inch vise.
pros: Enclosed greased spindle keeps dirt out of the screw
Replaceable hardened jaw faces extend its life
Double lockdowns hold the swivel base firmly
Six inch jaws suit most garage work
cons: Costs more than import ductile iron vises
Heavy to mount and move once installed

products.name: Wilton 8 inch reversible bench vise, opens to 14.5 inches, pipe jaws
products.description:
The Wilton 8 inch reversible vise has a head that can be flipped to open to 14 1/2 inches, compared with 9 1/4 inches in the normal position. That range lets you hold large pieces like engine parts, long stock or awkward fabrications.

The 8 inch jaws and built in pipe jaws make this a serious shop vise, and the 360 degree swivel with dual lockdowns lets you reposition the work. It sits at the top of the cost range here, which reflects both size and weight. Compared with the 746A, it is bigger and more capable but demands a stronger bench. Compared with the Forward CR80A, it offers a reversible head and a stronger reputation.

Ownership is about the bench. Mount through the top with grade 8 bolts and a steel backing plate, keep the screw oiled and store the head in whichever position you use most. Avoid hammering on the jaws.
products.bestFor: Shops handling large parts and long stock that need a wide opening.
pros: Reversible head opens to 14 1/2 inches
Eight inch jaws grip large work firmly
Built in pipe jaws hold round stock
Dual lockdowns on a 360 degree base
cons: Highest cost tier among the vises here
Very heavy and needs a sturdy bench

products.name: Yost Vises 760-DI 6 inch multi jaw rotating bench and pipe vise

specList.label: Material
specList.value: 60,000 psi ductile iron, per the maker

specList.label: Features
specList.value: Multi jaw, rotating head and body

products.description:
The Yost 760-DI is a 6 inch vise with a multi jaw design that doubles as a pipe vise, a 5.90 inch opening and a 4.31 inch throat depth. The body and head rotate 360 degrees, which allows you to turn the work without releasing it.

The maker cites 60,000 psi ductile iron, a tensile figure that is common among import vises and that we treat as a claim. Compared with the Wilton 746A, it has a deeper throat but a less proven spindle design. Compared with the VEVOR 6 inch, it is similar in capacity and the choice comes down to the brand reputation and finish.

Ownership is simple. Oil the screw regularly, keep the jaws clean of chips and replace worn inserts. Mount it with through bolts and avoid hammering on the jaw faces.
products.bestFor: General workshop use that needs both bench and pipe clamping.
pros: Deep 4.31 inch throat handles larger stock
Multi jaw design holds pipe and flat stock
Rotating head and body repositions the work
Ductile iron body resists cracking
cons: Open screw needs regular cleaning and oiling
Tensile figure is a maker claim

products.name: Forward CR80A 8 inch heavy duty bench vise with anvil, 210 degree swivel
products.description:
The Forward CR80A is an 8 inch ductile iron vise with a 9 inch opening, a 4.1 inch throat and an integrated anvil. The maker claims 12,000 pounds of clamping force, a figure without a shared test method, so we rate it by size and body mass.

The swivel base rotates 210 degrees rather than a full circle, which is enough for most positions and keeps the base simpler. Compared with the Wilton 8 inch, it is cheaper, lacks the reversible head and has a shorter record. Compared with the Forward DT08125A, it is a much larger vise that needs more bench strength.

Ownership is about mounting. Use bolts through the bench and a backing plate, keep the screw oiled and use the anvil for light shaping only. Do not hammer the jaws or use a cheater pipe on the handle.
products.bestFor: Metal workers who want a large ductile iron vise with an anvil.
pros: Eight inch jaws and a 9 inch opening
Integrated anvil for light shaping
Ductile iron body is stronger than gray iron
Lower cost than a Wilton of the same size
cons: Swivel is 210 degrees, not a full circle
Clamping force is a maker claim

products.name: Forward DT08125A 5 inch heavy duty bench vise, 360 degree swivel base and head
products.description:
The Forward DT08125A is a 5 inch vise with a 5 inch opening, a 2.6 inch throat and a swivel that turns the base and the head a full 360 degrees. It is aimed at metalworking in a small shop and costs less than a Wilton.

The shallow throat is the main limit, since it can only hold work that reaches about 2.6 inches into the jaws. The maker cites 5,500 pounds of clamping force and a stronger material than previous versions, both claims we leave unverified. Compared with the Yost 760-DI, it is smaller with a shallower throat, but more compact for a small bench. Compared with the PONY 4 inch, it has more capacity.

Ownership is simple. Oil the screw, keep chips out of the slides and tighten the base bolts after the first month. The compact size is easier to mount on a lightweight bench.
products.bestFor: Small shops and light benches that need a compact metalworking vise.
pros: Base and head both swivel through 360 degrees
Compact size suits lighter benches
Five inch jaws handle most small projects
Lower cost than premium vises
cons: Shallow 2.6 inch throat limits work size
Force figure is a maker claim

products.name: VEVOR 6 inch bench vise, 5.9 inch opening, 360 swivel, anvil and tool kit

specList.label: Material
specList.value: 60,000 psi ductile iron, per the maker

products.description:
The VEVOR 6 inch vise combines a 5.9 inch opening, a ductile iron body, a 2.9 by 3 inch anvil and a 360 degree swivel base with a locking system, plus a kit of accessories. It sits at a low cost tier, which makes it the value pick.

The anvil is a small flat area behind the jaws that is made for light hammering, though you should not strike the jaws or the screw. Compared with the Wilton 746A, the VEVOR has a similar capacity but less refined tolerances and an open screw. Compared with the Yost, the specs are very close and the choice depends on price.

Ownership requires basic care. Oil the screw, brush chips out of the guides and tighten the base bolts. If the slides feel rough out of the box, deburr them with a file and lubricate before use.
products.bestFor: Garage workshops that want a capable 6 inch vise at a low cost.
pros: Six inch jaws and 5.9 inch opening at a low cost
Built in anvil for light hammering
Full 360 degree swivel base
Ductile iron body resists cracking
cons: Open screw needs more cleaning than a sealed spindle
Tolerances are looser than premium brands

products.name: PONY 4 inch heavy duty bench vise, 360 rotation, dustproof screw
products.description:
The PONY 4 inch vise is a compact bench vise with a 360 degree rotating base and a dustproof screw design. The maker states a clamping force of 4400 pounds, which we treat as a claim and not a certified rating.

Four inch jaws are enough for light fabrication, model making, small engine parts and hobby work, but they will not hold large pieces. The dustproof screw helps keep chips out, an unusual feature at this cost. Compared with the Forward DT08125A, it is smaller and cheaper, and compared with the VEVOR 6 inch, it has much less capacity.

Ownership is simple. Oil the screw, tighten the base bolts and keep the vise out of damp areas. It is a good second vise for a small bench or a hobby corner.
products.bestFor: Hobbyists and small benches that need a compact vise.
pros: Compact four inch jaws fit a small bench
Dustproof screw design keeps chips out
Full 360 degree rotating base
Low cost tier for a swivel vise
cons: Four inch jaws cannot hold large work
Clamping figure is a maker claim

buyingCriteria.explanation: Jaw width labels the vise size, and opening and throat depth decide what fits. Four to five inches suit hobby work, 6 inches suits most garages and 8 inches suits large parts. Buyers often match the jaw width but forget the opening. The Wilton 746A has a 5 3/4 inch opening and the Wilton 8 inch opens to 14 1/2 inches reversed.

Gray cast iron is brittle and can crack when hammered, while ductile iron tolerates more abuse, and steel is the strongest. Tensile figures like 60,000 psi are maker claims. Ductile iron is the sweet spot for a home shop. The Yost, VEVOR and Forward vises use ductile iron.

A swivel base lets you reposition work, but a weak lock can let the vise rotate under force. Two lockdown bolts hold better than one. A 360 degree swivel is more flexible than a 210 degree one. The Wilton vises list double lockdowns.
An enclosed, greased spindle keeps chips and dust out of the screw and nut, which reduces wear and cleaning. Open screws work fine with regular oiling. The Wilton 746A has an enclosed spindle.

Replaceable hardened jaw faces extend a vise's life, and built in pipe jaws hold round stock. Soft jaw covers protect finished work. Check that the jaws line up and close flat. Most vises here include pipe jaws.

Listings quote clamping force in thousands of pounds without a shared test. The numbers vary from 4400 to 12,000 and tell you little. Judge a vise by body mass, screw size and build quality. We treat these figures as maker claims.

howWeEvaluated.title: Spec sheet review
howWeEvaluated.description: We evaluated jaw width, opening, throat depth, material and swivel design from each listing. We compared them with what a home shop clamps. The Wilton and Forward vises anchored the comparison.

howWeEvaluated.title: Owner feedback patterns
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked for repeating comments on cracked bodies, weak swivel locks, gritty screws and loose jaws. These issues decide whether a vise lasts. Swivel base slipping came up often.

howWeEvaluated.title: Fit for the bench
howWeEvaluated.description: A vise must suit the bench it is bolted to. We graded each product on size and weight, from the compact PONY to the heavy Wilton 8 inch.

howWeEvaluated.title: Cost relative to the lineup
howWeEvaluated.description: We used relative cost tiers and quote no listing prices. The VEVOR and PONY sit at the low end, while the Wilton 8 inch sits at the top.

howWeEvaluated.title: Claims we discounted
howWeEvaluated.description: Clamping force and tensile figures appear on most listings. We treat them as maker claims and rank on build and capacity.

cards.label: Premium brand
cards.text: Wilton offers enclosed spindles, replaceable jaws and a long record. The cost is higher.

cards.label: Import value
cards.text: VEVOR, Yost and Forward give similar jaw sizes in ductile iron for less, with looser tolerances and open screws.

howToChoose.note: Choose Wilton if you use a vise daily, and an import if the vise sees weekend work.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A ductile iron or steel body, hardened replaceable jaws, an anvil and a swivel base that locks firmly. Mount the vise near a bench leg.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Forward CR80A is the first choice for large work, with the Wilton 746A as the premium alternative.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You use the vise daily or work on large parts. Wilton builds last decades and keep their alignment.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: Your vise sees light weekend use. The VEVOR or PONY is enough.

maintenance.why: Chips and rust grind the screw and cause stiffness. A little machine oil keeps it smooth.

maintenance.interval: After the first month, then yearly
maintenance.why: Bolts loosen with vibration and clamping force. A loose base lets the vise shift under load.
Smooth jaws let work slip. New faces restore grip.

maintenance.task: Keep chips out of the guides
maintenance.why: Chips scratch the sliding parts. A brush and a blast of air clean them out.

maintenance.task: Do not hammer the jaws or handle
maintenance.why: Hammering cracks cast iron and bends screws. Use the anvil face only.

faq.q: What size bench vise should I buy?
faq.a: A 6 inch vise suits most garages, 4 to 5 inches suits hobby work and 8 inches suits large parts. Check the opening and throat depth as well.

faq.q: Is ductile iron better than cast iron?
faq.a: Yes. Ductile iron tolerates shock better and is less likely to crack. Gray cast iron is brittle.

faq.q: Can I hammer on a vise?
faq.a: Only on the anvil face. Hammering the jaws, screw or handle can crack the body or bend the screw.

faq.q: How should I mount a vise?
faq.a: Bolt it through the bench top with grade 8 bolts and a steel backing plate, near a leg. Do not use wood screws.
They are maker claims with no shared test. Judge a vise by body mass, screw size and build quality.
They are useful for round stock and pipe. Most vises here include them, so check before you buy.
